headline: Bangladesh public health facilities face severe medicine shortages and disrupted lab services, study finds
summary: A government study reveals that essential medicines are critically low, and diagnostic services are disrupted across public health facilities due to equipment failure, reagent shortages, and staff vacancies, leaving many without vital care.
details: Many public health facilities in Bangladesh are facing severe shortages of essential medicines, while diagnostic laboratory services remain disrupted. This is due to non-functional equipment, reagent shortages, and a lack of trained personnel, depriving many citizens of access to crucial healthcare services.

These findings come from a government-funded study conducted by the Power and Participation Research Centre (PPRC) on behalf of the Health Economics Unit. Data was collected from 22 public health facilities, including district hospitals and upazila health complexes, between August and October last year.

Lab service disruptions are significant, with 43 percent caused by reagent stock-outs and another 34 percent by non-functional equipment. A shortage of trained medical technologists accounts for 19 percent of these diagnostic service interruptions.

Despite relatively high nominal availability of imaging services, sustained availability remains low, ranging from 17-33 percent. This underutilization is largely due to non-functional equipment (79 percent), shortages of consumables (14 percent), and personnel (7 percent).

The availability of essential medicines is critically low, standing at just 22.7 percent at upazila health complexes and 23.9 percent at district hospitals. Tertiary hospitals fare even worse, with only 11.5 percent availability, a trend that has persisted over the past year.

About 62 percent of medicines supplied to public health facilities come from the government-run Essential Drugs Company (EDCL). However, EDCL's limited production capacity, reliance on imported raw materials, and weak distribution systems hinder consistent supply.

While routine medical supplies like gauze and cotton are widely available, many facilities lack critical emergency supplies. 64 percent reported no tourniquets, 55 percent lacked bag-valve-mask resuscitators, and 41 percent were without umbilical cord clamps, posing risks to emergency and maternal care.

A significant challenge is the severe shortage of medical technologists, with nearly 40 percent of sanctioned posts under the ministry remaining vacant. Vacancy rates are 36 percent at tertiary hospitals, 27 percent at upazila health complexes, and 12 percent at secondary hospitals.

More than 20 percent of development spending went to constructing new facilities, many of which remained non-operational for years. This was due to staff shortages, delayed handovers, and failure to meet required standards, yet new construction projects continued to receive approval.

Despite 94 percent of facilities ending the fiscal year with unspent funds, only 11 percent identified financial mismanagement as a problem. The report attributed underspending to administrative and governance challenges, including fear of audit objections and rigid procurement rules.

headline_marked: [[Textile mill production halved]] amid gas crisis, millers seek PM's urgent intervention
headline: Textile mill production halved amid gas crisis, millers seek PM's urgent intervention
summary: Bangladesh's $25 billion primary textile sector faces severe challenges, including a critical gas shortage, leading to significant production cuts and urgent calls for government action.
details: Bangladesh's textile mill production has reportedly been nearly halved over the past week due to a severe gas crisis. Textile millers yesterday urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman for an immediate solution to this pressing issue.

The demand was raised during a meeting with the premier in Dhaka, highlighting the multifaceted challenges facing the nearly $25 billion primary textile sector. These include the gas crisis, business safety concerns, and cheap yarn imports.

Prime Minister Rahman assured the millers that the government is actively working to install two more floating storage and regasification units (FSRUs). This initiative aims to alleviate the ongoing gas shortage across the country.

Showkat Aziz Russell, BTMA president, also mentioned discussions on the troubled banking sector and high interest rates. He announced a follow-up meeting with the PM, involving leaders from BGMEA and BKMEA, within weeks.

Earlier, BGMEA and BKMEA had demanded uninterrupted gas supply, even from CNG filling stations, as garment factories relying on CNG faced repeated disruptions. Many factories resorted to buying CNG from nearby stations to maintain operations.

Titas Gas had previously instructed CNG stations to stop selling gas into open cylinders, citing safety concerns. However, the Energy Secretary later directed Titas Gas to allow garment factories to continue collecting gas from these stations.

CNG filling station owners are currently supplying gas to garment factories despite it not being technically permitted for lorry-load sales. This highlights the desperate measures taken by the industry to sustain production.
